rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 OBJECTIVE 2 SETUP 3 GAMEPLAY 4 KEY CONCEPTS 5 END OF GAME OBJECTIVE Recruit adventurers for your guild, optimize your formation, and collect the most Victory Points (VP) through combat, technology, magic, and fulfilling quests. SETUP Each player receives a player board and 4 markers (Combat, VP, Technology, Magic). Place the shared Combat and Victory board in the center. Each player starts with 3 Money and a starting hand of 5 cards . Display the Quest cards face-up. GAMEPLAY Each round consists of 6 phases, played simultaneously: 1. Discard & Draw Phase: Discard any number of hand cards and draw back up to 5 cards . 2. Recruit Phase: You may play 0 /1 / 2 cards from your hand by paying their cost (top left) in gold. Each card not played earns 1 gold. Place it in your 3x3 grid, orthogonally adjacent to an existing card. Complete the recruit effects and link bonuses for the cards that were played. 3. Combat Phase: Compare your Combat Power with all other players. The stronger player(s) receives VP based on the player count. Example: In a 5-player game, if two players are tied for first place, they each receive 5 VP. Any second place players receive 1 VP instead of 3. Players in third, fourth, and fifth place will receive no VP 4. Production Phase: Every Adventurer with the Production symbol activates that line of text now. Most Production involves adding Magic and Technology. 5. Income Phase: Gain 3 Money. Then look for any of your recruited Adventurers with the Income icon ; you gain extra Money as specified on their cards. 6. Victory Point Phase: Look for any of your recruited Adventurers with the VP icon , and gain that many VPs. KEY CONCEPTS Factions: There are 6 different factions (e.g., Floating City, Mining Company) essential for line bonuses. Professions: Warrior, Wizard, Merchant, etc., also determine synergies within the grid. Tech & Magic: These tracks grant additional victory points at the end of the game or via card effects. Resources: Symbols on cards that provide permanent cost reductions for recruiting. END OF GAME The game ends at the end the round where a player has 9 cards in their grid or a player reaches 40 VPs . Every 3 remaining money converts to 1 VP. The player with the most VP wins.

[Rating: 3/10] I don't like this game, for it is luck dependent and with a light engine building that is both comboastic and a disastrous.  It is impossible to stop the running leader, and there are no catch up mechanisms. The war highly worsen this idea. I don't suggest it

[Rating: 4/10] After 2 games on BGA: This is purely a matter of personal taste, but I find the illustrations kind of ugly. The art style is just not my thing at all. Optimizing the cards feels strangely soulless to me. I don't feel much desire to invest thought into it. I can imagine, though, that some people might find it quite satisfying to watch their tableau gradually improve and generate points in different ways.

[Rating: 5/10] OK little tableau game. + plays reasonably quickly - little interaction  - very dependant on which cards you draw

[Rating: 5/10] These tableau/grid builders seem to be getting popular these days (this has a max 3x3 grid). This one works as well as any of the others do but nothing about it really gripped me.  It likewise plays quite quickly.  It does have some importance where you place your cards - the top card in each column is used to determine your strength which is compared to other players each round.  The only other significant aspect of placement to keep in mind is that if a row/column has one color in common (each card has two associated colors) the player gets to take a bonus from the bottom of one of the cards

[Rating: 5/10] nice artwork but rather than a draft of some sort, your options are to keep or discard and redraw--hoping for something better. Card combo games benefit from having a bit more player interactivity. It plays quickly though.

[Rating: 5/10] Eh, another 3x3 tableau builder - plays super fast with simultaneous turns, but there is essentially no interaction (you are comparing combat values, but it's not easy to know what the other player has in advance, unlike say 7 Wonders).  Nothing really exciting to me.

[Rating: 5/10] Unbalanced game with a lot of luck and not a lot of skill involved. There are much better games in this category.

[Rating: 5/10] 06/2026: Ach, „Yro“, was mache ich nur mit dir? Vor den zwei Partien hatte ich so viel Gutes von dir vernommen. Kleine Tableau-Builder, wie ich sie von zahlreichen anderen Titeln kenne, machen mir normalerweise Spaß. Dazu im Manga-Chibi-Stil von Takashi Konno auf den Karten. So etwas liebe ich normalerweise. Und dann traf ich auf ein Spiel, in welchem es scheinbar nur darum geht, irgendwelche Extremstrategien zu suchen.  „Yro“ ist ein Tableau- und Engine-Builder, bei dem ich Handkarten in ein Raster vor mir ausspiele. Jede Runde läuft dabei identisch ab und alle spielen parallel: Zuerst unpass

[Rating: 5/10] A tableau building game, players play throw a bunch of phases (draw back up to 5 cards, play 1-2 card(s), fight your opponents, gain points, magic/tech levels, money. Players are going to build a 3x3 grid, much like kingdominio, if the icons in a row or column are all the same, players gain the benefit. Players keep playing rounds until a player builds a 3x3 grid or 40 points is scored, then the player with the most points wins.

[Rating: 5/10] Schöne Illustration im Anime-Style. Jeder wählt 1 oder 2 Karten aus der Hand aus, um sie vor sich in ein 3x3-Raster zu legen. Durch Eigenschaften der ausgelegten Charaktere erhält man Punkte. Wenn 3 Charaktere derselben Gruppe in einer Reihe oder Zeile liegen, gibt es Extrapunkte. Jeder spielt für sich – bis auf den Vergleich der Krampfkrampf gitb es keine Interaktion.
